newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- U.S. inflation steady two years out.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- U.S. inflation steady two years out.

text.p: Inflation will remain under control in the United States over the next two years, despite rising wages and a low unemployment. That key inflation measure should hover near 3.0 percent going forward into late 1998, they said.
Separately, the experts forecast the overall Producer Price Index (PPI) would expand at a 2.5 percent rate in the current quarter and then increase about 2.3 percent annually into 1998.
Between September 1995 and September 1996, core CPI grew 2.7 percent and PPI rose 2.9 percent, according to the Labor Department.

"Essentially no change in inflation is how I would summarize the outlook," said Kurt Karl, chief economist of U.S. forecasting at WEFA Group. "We've reached a balance between wage gains and productivity gains."
Average hourly earnings have increased about 3.6 percent in the first nine months of 1996 to $11.92. By contrast, earnings rose about 2.9 percent in all of 1995.
The Federal Reserve has said it keeps close watch over wage-related inflation, but many survey respondents said earnings increases do not necessarily lead to higher inflation in general.

"As much as we've heard about the relationship between inflation and wages, recent studies by the Dallas Fed and the San Francisco Fed found there really is no link between higher wages and higher inflation," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Securities Inc.
In a separate portion of the quarterly survey, economists projected the unemployment rate would rebound slowly to 5.5 percent by late 1998 from 5.2 percent last month.

"Employment growth will ... continue to trend downward from the relatively fast pace in the first half of this year, and therefore wages (will) slow down," said Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch Government Securities Inc.
The eventual addition of welfare recipients to the labor force, coupled with expected slower payrolls growth, will account for a portion of the gradual jobless rate uptick, economists said.
Forecasts for such relatively high employment with benign price growth might suggest the theoretical Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment, or NAIRU, is lower than traditionally thought.
"Although we are seeing some wage creep in here ... companies are unable to pass on those wage increases (to consumers)," Katz said. "Rather, it's a bite out of profit margins."
She added that "the natural rate of unemployment is probably closer to 5.0 (percent) rather than 5.5."
